TELNET · DNS · FTP · HTTP · SNMP · SMTP …

It is called a suite because it is a set of protocols; among them, TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and IP (Internet Protocol).

  • Network layer: the protocol is IP. The others (ARP, RARP, ICMP…) are supporting protocols: they help IP.
  • Transport: two variants, TCP (the reliable one) and UDP (the agile one).
  • Application: above transport, all the well-known protocols (HTTP, DNS, FTP, SMTP…).
Many applications on top, many networks below and, in the middle, a single network protocol: IP.

Everything operates on a connectionless packet delivery service. At the network layer we talk about packets or datagrams. IP's service is:

  • Unreliable: packets may be lost, duplicated, reordered or delayed, and IP does not notify the receiver.
  • Connectionless: each packet is treated independently. Routers keep no state about what they did with the previous one or what they will do with the next one.
  • Best effort: there are no guarantees.

In exchange it is resilient: it recovers from any network failure.
IP does its best with each packet, separately and promising nothing.
Three packets of the same message: each one is routed separately. Packet 2 arrives before 1 and 3 is lost, with no one notified.

The protocol is implemented in the header, which is drawn in 32-bit rows. The first two fields:

  • Version (4 bits).
  • HLEN (4 bits): header length, which can be variable. It is measured in 32-bit words, and the minimum is 5 words.

With HLEN you know what part of the total datagram is header and where the data begins.
HLEN does not count bytes: it counts 32-bit rows.
HLEN = 5 → 5 words × 32 bits = 160 bits = 20 bytes: the first five rows of the drawing. If there are options, HLEN is larger.
Total length and the fragmentation fields

• Total length (16 bits): size of the whole datagram. With 16 bits, the maximum value is 65,535.
  • Identification: each packet leaving the host carries a different value; it is its own identifier.
  • Flags and Offset (fragment offset): together with the identification they allow a datagram to be split and put back together.

Those three fields are the topic of the next lesson: fragmentation.
An IP datagram can be at most 65,535 bytes long.
Total length: 16 bits → from 0 to 2¹⁶ − 1 = 65,535. Identification + Flags + Offset take up the whole second row: 16 + 3 + 13 = 32 bits.

• Protocol (8 bits): indicates what is in the data field; for example, a TCP segment.
  • Checksum (16 bits): used to detect errors, but only in the header. IP does not guarantee error-free delivery: it only checks that the header is correct.

If there is an error in the header, the datagram is discarded: we cannot be sure it is going to the right destination.
The IP checksum protects the header, not the data.
A single flipped bit in the destination address would send the datagram elsewhere: that is why, on a bad checksum, the router discards it without trying to fix it.

• Source and destination IP address (32 bits each).
  • Options: these are what make the header length variable.
  • Padding: fills out the options field so it takes up all the bits of the word (similar to Ethernet padding).

IP serves two functions: with the addresses it identifies who I am and where I want to go, and with routing it works out how to get there.
Addressing and routing: IP's two tasks.
Without options, the header ends at the destination address (20 bytes, HLEN = 5). With options, the padding brings it up to a multiple of 32 bits so HLEN can count it.

Time To Live (8 bits): originally, a maximum lifetime of 255 seconds. Each router was supposed to subtract the time the datagram spent in its queues or being processed.

What is done today is simpler: each router decrements it by 1. It went from seconds to hops: how many routers it can cross before running out of life.

It serves to prevent loops, where datagrams go around without making progress. When the TTL reaches 0, the router discards it.
The TTL is a hop counter: it guarantees no datagram circulates forever.
A routing error creates a loop among R1, R2 and R3. Without TTL the datagram would circle forever; with TTL, the router that drops it to 0 discards it.
Type of Service: marking the packet

ToS (8 bits) implements, in a way, the idea of quality of service: marking packets with an indicator of how they should be treated (urgent, can wait…).

Originally 4 bits were defined; later, various RFCs modified them and added others. Only one of the four can be set:

  • Minimize delay
  • Maximize throughput
  • Maximize reliability
  • Minimize cost
Each application marks what matters most to it: Telnet asks for low delay; FTP data, high throughput.

Routers do routing: they connect networks until reaching the destination. If they switch looking only at the destination address, nothing more needs to be said to them.

But the protocol allows influencing that decision. When a router has two paths to the destination, depending on the ToS the packet can take the fastest, the cheapest, etc.

Careful: each router also has its own customers. A packet marked urgent conflicts with their packets. It is a very fragile system.
Asking for special treatment does not oblige anyone: each network along the path has its own priorities.
My urgent packet competes with the packets of each provider's customers. This must be taken into account before influencing the path.
The IP datagram at a glance

• IP is connectionless, unreliable and best effort: each datagram travels on its own.
  • Header of at least 20 bytes (HLEN = 5); datagram of up to 65,535 bytes.
  • TTL: each router subtracts 1; at 0 it is discarded.
  • Checksum: header only.
  • ToS: 4 bits to ask for less delay, more throughput, more reliability or lower cost.

Identification, Flags and Offset remain pending. In the next lesson we see what they are for: fragmentation and reassembly.
